utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning to you all. In the first stage of the morning, we will hear any submissions that counsel feel they wish to put in addition to the written submissions on the question of the fitness of the accused to stand trial. It's your motion, I think, so that you should have first submission, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, the Defence in its attachment in the motion is asking for these proceedings to be stopped because of the inability of the accused Pavle Strugar to follow the proceedings here and submitted a medical report by Dr. Dusica Lecic-Tosevski. It was submitted on the 1st of February with another addition on the 12th of February this year. Besides that, the Defence on the 4th of May submitted its written submission regarding the clarification of certain important circumstances regarding the procedural fitness of the accused before the Chamber. The Defence wishes to say that it will just briefly address you in this situation, that it stands by everything in the reports, the report of the 2nd of February and the continuation of that report of the 12th of February, as well as by what was stated during the proceedings of last week when we heard the experts of the Defence and the Prosecution. The Defence stands by everything that it stated there. The Defence would first like to say that it thinks that the medical report submitted on behalf of the Defence was drafted in accordance with the rules of the profession, the methodology replied in drafting the report is clear, consistent, and that the conclusions arising the report are beyond doubt. The Defence is even more convinced in the correctness of what is stated in Dr. Lecic-Tosevski's report following the questioning, the cross-examination by the Prosecution, because this only boiled down to an attempt to disqualify what the Defence expert stated in their motions and what she said during her examination. There were diagnoses, and the diagnostic methods applied in the drafting of the reports of the 2nd and the 12th were not brought into question through the questions of our learned colleagues. And they were not put into question in such a way which would prevent Your Honours from basing your decisions on what Dr. Lecic-Tosevski found in her reports. Your Honours, we believe that there is one thing on which we can all agree. I believe that this arises also from the position of the Prosecution in this matter. And that is as follows: General Pavle Strugar is a person with very serious health problems. I think that we agree on that, and this also arises from what is stated in the reports by the Prosecution. The Defence expert witness established that General Pavle Strugar is not fit to follow the proceedings and that he's not fit for reasons of numerous illnesses that he is suffering from. General Pavle Strugar suffers from dementia, from depression, from PTSD. Also, he has chronic kidney insufficiency. He has spondyloarthrosis and other illnesses which were stated in the reports, primarily the reports by the Defence and which were indirectly also confirmed through the findings of those by the Prosecution. All of these illnesses individually and together make General Pavle Strugar a person who is not able to follow the proceedings before this Honourable Tribunal. Dementia, which General Pavle Strugar suffers from, of course, affects his memory, his ability of recollection, memorising new things, and recalling old things, things that were learned before. Depression and PTSD affect also his attention span, his concentration, his ability to plan and conceive what is supposed to be the defence of General Pavle Strugar before this Chamber. Chronic kidney disease, from which General Pavle Strugar is suffering, affects the levels of uria and creatine in his blood and affects the level of poisons or toxins in his blood which are constantly poisoning his brain, his nervous system, and making his functioning more difficult as well as damaging his mental and other functions. Spondyloarthrosis is a disease which, as one of its consequences, has the more difficult nourishing of the brain which affects his speech ability which for a person of his age and his overall health situation is already below normal. Another effect is also the effect of spondyloarthrosis [as interpreted]. So the individual effect of each of these diseases boil down to the fact that he is not able to follow the proceedings at a level that is essential. General Strugar is required to follow the proceedings for five days a week, and for the past five or six months back he was required to actively take part in these proceedings, to follow everything that is being said in this courtroom, to be attentive, to remember that, to write it down, to analyse it. He is being also required to be able to, after 13 years with all of these diagnoses that have been given and which cannot be questioned, he's being asked to reconstruct the events that are being discussed here, to remember the names of the protagonists in those events, to remember their role in those events, to recall his own role in those events. All of this is important and for him to know so that at any point he has all his -- this information at his fingertips as well as his Defence so we can react timely in any situation that occurs in this courtroom. General Strugar is also being expected to testify. He's expected before this Honourable Trial Chamber to talk -- to give the truth about the events he is being charged with. He is expected to be efficacious in being submitted to a cross-examination by the Prosecution, to respond to all types of questions, to respond to questions in a time interval which would last from a few days or even longer. And also, what is being asked of him is, because of his illness, to be brought in a legally inferior position. Can we ask this of him in view of all the illnesses that he has been diagnosed with? And this is something that is not being questioned. None of these functions that we discussed is General Strugar able to fulfil effectively at the level required so that he does not jeopardise his legal position before this Trial Chamber. The Defence at no point in time claimed that General Strugar is so disabled that he's not able to understand that he's in a courtroom, that he's before the International Tribunal and that he's being brought to trial. This is not something that the Defence disputes. The Defence doubts his ability to actively follow these proceedings in a satisfactory manner. It is not in dispute that General Strugar understands what the United Nations are, but it is disputable whether General Strugar can in an efficient manner process tens of -- scores of hundreds of pieces of information that have been stated in this courtroom over the past few months. Can he draw synthetic conclusions from everything that he hears? Can he advise us regarding the events that he is being charged with? Can he testify without falling into the trap which can to a large extent make his procedural position more difficult? The only thing that General Strugar unfortunately is able to discuss effectively and comprehensively with his lawyer is his medical condition, his health problems. The question of, as he said just before the beginning of these proceedings this morning, that he has quite serious pain in his hip, that he's suffering, like he said yesterday, from toothache or that he told us last week that he did not sleep for two days in a row. So unfortunately, this is what the communication between us, the Defence of General Pavle Strugar, and him boils down to. The confirmation of what I'm saying here can be found in Dr. Lecic-Tosevski's report. Her conclusion, and you have that before you, is that the combination of psychological and somatic illnesses that General Strugar is suffering from is making more difficult to a considerable extent his memory, concentration, attention, planning, and strategy. If we analyse some conditions which are relevant in assessing his procedural fitness, and those are whether the accused understands the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. indictment, whether he understands the proceedings, whether he's able to instruct his lawyers, whether he's able to testify, and whether he's able to understand the consequences of his conviction. The answers to all of these questions for the most part are that he is not fit to do this. Your Honours, the Defence believes that the confirmation of what the Defence position is is also found in the views of the Prosecution expert witnesses. When we look at those more closely, we see there that General Pavle Strugar suffers from vascular dementia. There is no disagreement between the sides on the fact that General Strugar suffers from vascular dementia. He's a person suffering from vascular dementia. At this point, this Trial Chamber is conducting proceedings against a person suffering from vascular dementia, and this is what is stated also in the Prosecution witness's report. Their experts state in several places that General Strugar forgets places, that he forgets their names already after several hours, even though they were told to him several times. At a standard psychological ability test, he was given three simple concepts or terms to remember. Out of those three simple terms when he was asked following -- immediately following after he was given them, he could not interpret two of those terms, two of three that he was given he was not able to remember. Nobody disputed, Your Honour, at any point whether General Strugar was sincere, whether he was absolutely open in what he said, and in his cooperation, both with the experts of the Defence and the Prosecution. So he was not able to remember two out of a total of three terms. Can such a person remember names of witnesses? Can he operatively use the names of those witnesses when talking to his attorneys? Can he use those names efficiently in his possible testimony? If out of three terms, he forgets two after half an hour, can he effectively use the contents of the testimonies before this Trial Chamber to recall them, to recall from his memory names of witnesses or to recall a situation or an event and refer to it and talk about it? Prosecution expert witness, from the facts that the accused has general cognizance of where he is, what is being discussed here, who the Judges are, who the Prosecution is, who the Defence is, what the United Nations is, from these general pieces of information and from this knowledge of General Strugar, the witness draws the conclusion that these general concepts are being interpreted as him being fit to follow the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, I'm going to have to ask you to draw to a close.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you can permit me just two more minutes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: One more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. The essence of what the Prosecution expert witnesses say is that there is vascular dementia, but they bring in a completely unknown category in the medical sciences. They categorise vascular dementia, claiming that there is a milder case of such dementia or a grave case of such dementia. This is something that medical sciences do not know. They're doing something to try to minimise his ailment. Even the accused himself, General Strugar, minimises his own disability. This is what Dr. Lecic said. He's used to suffering hardships. He's used to not showing that he's in pain or that he's suffering. This is due to his upbringing, due to his years. Your Honours, there is no dispute that you have before you a person suffering from vascular dementia. The reasons from general legal principles and also enshrined in the Statute of the International Tribunal and for reasons of justice and humanity urge you, Your Honours, to reach a decision granting the request of the Defence to stop with these proceedings. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, Mr. Re will speak for the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The Prosecution's submission is that the accused is fit for trial. The Prosecution has -- had engaged three eminent psychiatrists to examine the accused. They applied the standard tests which are used in assessing competency in domestic jurisdictions, and they found him fit to stand trial. Against that, we had one Defence psychiatrist who applied basically what appears to be her own medical diagnostic definition or test who declared him to be unfit. In summary, the Prosecution says there is simply no evidence that the accused is unfit under standard competency tests to stand trial. The Prosecution's submission is that these tests are to be found or best summarised in the two extracts which we tendered in the proceedings last week and are referred to in the psychiatric tests of both sets of psychiatrists. The first time -- one is the Gruso [phoen] test set out in evaluating competencies, forensic assessments and instruments. We've annexed that to the written submissions filed yesterday. The things the Court should be looking at or the Trial Chamber should be examining in determining or assessing competency are set out there. You must look in our submission at each of those and determine whether or not there is evidence of these things. The Prosecution's submission backed by the evidence of the joint psychiatric report is that there is no evidence that the accused does not understand that counsel works for the Defence, that he doesn't understand counsel's inquiries; that is, not that he's uncapable of responding to counsel's inquiries in a manner providing relevant information for the Defence. There's evidence that he can provide a consistent account of events relevant to the charges and the Defence, that he can manage the trial process, and that he's capable of testifying. Professor Matthews gave evidence in cross-examination that he was capable of testifying. There is also no evidence the accused does not understand that he is faced or accused of a crime, that the Court will decide on guilt or innocence, that the trial could result in punishment, of his options in pleading, that certain sentences are possible; that is, the nature and seriousness, and of the various roles of the participants and the trial process. There's no evidence he that the defendant is unaware or unable to comprehend any of the things I've just listed or indeed the general process of the trial. There is no evidence that the accused's beliefs about the trial processes were distorted by any delusional beliefs. There is evidence that he is appropriate -- that he has appropriate motivations to further his own Defence and that his reasoning ability is sufficient to process the relevant information during the decision-making. Why do we say this? We say that because the methodology applied by the respective psychiatric teams in assessing the accused and his competence. Both psychiatrists of the Defence and Prosecution reviewed the medical history of the accused which is, of course, the correct thing to do. Dr. Lecic for the Defence then performed a battery of psychological tests none of which were specific to or designed in any way to assess trial competency or cognitive ability for trial competency. Dr. Blum, an expert in geriatric cognitive issues for the Prosecution, performed diagnostic tests. Professor Matthews who, as you heard, is an expert who has examined hundreds of people in competency hearings and works almost solely in this -- or works predominantly in this area, then assessed the history attained through Dr. Smaltz [phoen] and assessed the accused's standing against the standard competency tests. Dr. Lecic didn't do that. The Defence doctor didn't do that. The Prosecution also took another approach where they sought objective third-party history, in this case, prison guards. Dr. Lecic went to the accused's family. The Prosecution psychiatrist also looked at videos of the Court proceedings showing the interaction between the accused and the Court, his counsel and his speaking to the Court. The Prosecution's submission is that the -- as set out -- as shown in the cross-examination or the testimony of Dr. Blum and Dr. Matthews is that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the psychological tests administered by Professor Lecic are simply irrelevant to the task which she had before her. Of course, there is concurrence on the fact that the accused has a vascular dementia of some point. But the level of departure is at what point and whether or not it affects his cognitive abilities such as to prevent him from participating in the trial and understanding the proceedings. The Prosecution's psychiatrists, three eminent psychiatrists, found that the level was so mild that it did not impair his abilities. Dr. Lecic, on the other hand, leaped to a conclusion that because there was a diagnosis of some mild form of vascular dementia, therefore the accused was unfit to stand trial because he had a number of medical conditions at the same time. This of course confuses diagnosis with the condition -- with the cognitive ability to understand the trial proceedings. Dr. Lecic also diagnosed post-traumatic stress disorder in the accused, and she turned to the DSM-IV to determine that he had, in fact, this diagnosis. The DSM-IV criteria which he attached to her report and which he must meet to satisfy the diagnosis says that the accused was "exposed to an event in which the following were present." The DSM-IV text revision actually says "both of the following were present." One, he experienced, witnessed, and confronted events that involved actual death of many people as well as a threat to his physical integrity, et cetera; and two, his response involved intense fear and helplessness. Now, there is simply no evidence in the reports submitted or in the evidence that the accused had either of those two responses. The closest it seems to get is at page 5 of Professor Lecic's report where she refers to a single incident which the accused's son describes the accused as having spoken about. There is nothing in her history taken from the accused which gets anywhere near his recounting anything that happened to him during the war. In fact, it is almost the opposite. Her conclusion is that he has almost no memory of the war. That is, of course, completely contrary to the detailed history given to the Prosecution's psychiatrists. Professor Lecic did not explore with the accused - and she said this in cross-examination - ways that he could plead, the general trial process, his knowledge that certain sentences were possible. She did not ask his family, the so-called objective sources, about their understanding of his understanding of the trial process. In cross-examination, she said she discussed punishment and that it could decide on guilt and innocence. It doesn't appear in her report. She said that his memory was so impaired that he was not able to participate actively at a high level in these sophisticated proceedings. But how could she have known this if she didn't ask him the basic questions relating to the conduct or course of the trial? She concluded in cross-examination that he understands where he is -- I'm sorry, in examination-in-chief, what's going on, and what he has been accused of, but basically little more. Against that, the joint report showed the accused was able to choose his own lawyers, a military lawyer, an English-speaking lawyer. That is making a tactical choice. He explained to them in detail the nature of his defence, how it related to command responsibility. He explained the military hierarchy. He explained how he voluntarily surrendered. He explained how he, General Strugar, saved Dubrovnik and how Admiral Jokic was responsible for the destruction. He explained that Jokic was guilty, not he. He gave details of how he would testify. He named Prosecution witnesses. He referred to specific people, Mr. Vlasica, Mr. Valjalo, Mrs. Ogresta's testimony, and named two people, one of whom was Mr. Jusic. He explained about UNESCO, the Geneva Conventions. The Prosecution described him as having a rich vocabulary and an intelligent person. The Prosecution asked: Are they talking about the same person, the person who the Defence psychiatrist described as passive, lacking interest, helpless, and regressed to a helpless state? In conclusion, the Prosecution says that the only conclusion available when you examine the two reports and the testimony of both is that the accused has the necessary cognitive functions to stand trial, to continue trial, and that the Prosecution experts' reports and conclusions should be preferred to that of the Defence. And the Prosecution submits that you should find him fit for trial and dismiss the motion.

utterances.text: Building at 21.01, which building is that, showing some damage to the door frames?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I am familiar with this. This is the block near St. Blaise's church, and it is opposite the municipality building. We actually call the area Pred Dvorom. This is the ground floor of a building where there were two shops. It can be seen even on this still. It's a souvenir shop.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's the completion of the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukovic, for that. Now, I want you to turn to Exhibit 61, 39 which should have been provided to you. It's a commission Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. report on damage to old parts of Dubrovnik dated the 9th of December 1991 signed by Admiral Jokic. It's a JNA report of damage to the Old Town of the 6th of December. Just take a minute to read through that and familiarise yourself with the document. Have you familiarised yourself with the document, Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have had a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: At item 3, do you know -- or paragraph 3, the house of Rudjer Boskovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do know it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's in Boskoviceva Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that one of the houses we saw in the video showing the damage to the --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it was in the earlier footage. I think we saw it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want -- have you read the comment or the conclusion at the bottom, second-last paragraph "it is the opinion of the commission that there is no substantial damage to the cultural and historical monuments"?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: And just above that: "The town representative said there was no damage from the south of the Ulica Od Puca Street and that part of the town was no inspected." How does the assessment in that report compare with your own observations and inspections of the damage to the Old Town? You went there on the 7th of December and went around inspecting 63-odd structures between the 10th of December and the first week of January. How does what they say compare with what you saw as to the extent and level of damage?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will say two things. First of all, this report, I think, does not reflect even closely the real situation. That is one thing. The other thing is for this document to be reliable, especially as regards to the statements of gentlemen from the Institute for the Preservation of Cultural Monuments, they would need to analyse this and they would need to co-sign. The third thing is that the time given from 10.00 to 1400 hours, so to make an inspection in two hours of such a large job I think would cause perhaps some failings in this document or mistakes to be made, perhaps, or shortcomings to appear. So this is all that I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vukovic. Now, to complete your evidence-in-chief, I want to show you a plan of the Old Town, an overhead view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if my learned friend would ask the witness to mark anything, then I think the proper way to do it would be to provide the witness with an unmarked map. As far as I can see, what he has been given already has some red and orange markings. The map is already marked. So if he intends the witness to mark something he should provide him with an unmarked map. In this way, I believe we're proceeding in an improper way. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic knows exactly what I'm going to do. I've explained it to him out of court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That seems to give rise to the objection, not answer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm simply -- what we have done is the OTP has scanned a map of the Old Town. And we have plotted in red all the buildings that Mr. Vukovic inspected by himself or in combination with Mr. Kunic -- sorry, Ms. Kunic, or Mr. Vetma. And in orange, the buildings which are in map P174 as having been inspected by him and Mrs. Peko. It is simply an aide memoire to the Chambers to show where the buildings that he inspected are on the map of Dubrovnik. I'm not asking the witness to mark anything on this map. And Mr. Petrovic knows that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Subject to what you have put being the evidence of the witness, the document can be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, as explained to His Honour a moment ago, that is a document of which we've plotted in red the buildings you inspected in combination with others, and in orange those you inspected with Mrs. Peko. Is it accurate?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Only with one remark: Not shown here are buildings in black which burned down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I see some black-marked areas, Mr. Re, on the document. I don't know whether they are in any way related to the comment of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The black buildings are those the institute mark on the map as having been burnt down. Six of those are referred to in the indictment. Mr. Vukovic, I think, inspected one or two of those but they are not in the schedule of the indictment. The purpose of this exhibit is to match his buildings to those in the schedule. He's given oral evidence of inspecting those two buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You're saying a lot. At the moment, at least in my mind, there has been no connection between the black markings of which there appear to be five, not six, and the evidence of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, the black markings, what are they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The black markings show buildings which were entirely burned down. But in this image that we have here, as far as I am interpreting it, there are some buildings from the Od Puca Street which also burned down and which I inspected. I'm a little bit confused because there is one building there within the block that I inspected. It's marked in black and it did burn down. But there is yet another building and another building and yet another building which completely burned down. I don't know why they are not marked in black just like this other building. So please allow this to be my interpretation of this image.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Could the witness be offered a black pen and asked to put a cross on the buildings he says were burnt down. Is that a way?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I think the wiser would be for us to eliminate the black one and retender it later. We want a representation of the buildings he inspected, not those in black. I can do that, we can basically do that straight away, fairly quickly. I apologise for this. One slipped in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, it would perhaps help the Chamber if the buildings that are shown in red that had burnt down also had a black cross on them. The witness could do that now, and we can readily identify the one black stranger in the presently marked buildings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: His Honour has suggested a very, very good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Can you please just mark the black cross the buildings you inspected within the red area that burnt down. Or orange.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a building that partially burned down, and I will mark that in a special way. I will just like to note that this building was marked in our maps as partially burnt, meaning that the upper floor and the roof burn down. What was additionally marked now are buildings that burned down entirely including this building that was marked in black. So that would be all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think the record should record that the building pointed to by the witness as having burned in the roof and upper floors rather than in totality was at the left hand immediately of the one black building that is within the red-marked group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that on Od Puca Street, Mr. Vukovic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a corner building, Siroka Ulica, and the street Od Puca.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Did you mark on the building that was completely burned down that you inspected, the one in Miha Pracata?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's this building here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That's a building around the corner from Od Puca in Miha Pracata on the southern side. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is Nikola Gucetic Street and Miha Pracata Street. It's on the intersection. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The record might also be clearer if you would, Mr. Vukovic, point with that pen to the one building which you inspected which is shown on this plan as in black rather than red, having totally burnt down as I understand your evidence just so that we can be sure that we identify the same building as you do. Is that a building in Od Puca Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's what you are talking about. That's this building here. It's at that address. It's in Od Puca Street.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And it's in a block that is substantially in red, the most extreme left block of that nature on the plan. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I understood your question properly, if you're thinking of the blocks which were used in order to identify them, according to our methodology, I think that that is that block. I think then that this is block number 11.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now I think it would be useful if the Court officer in due course was able to reproduce on each of the Chamber's copies the markings from the marked exhibit so that we have accurate depictions, and the Defence counsel may want their map marked in the same way. Subject to that, do I understand you tender this map, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I do. But what we might -- what we could do, which might be better, is we could put -- go back and put a black X on these three buildings he just described and give it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There were more than three.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I will check the transcript. Yes, I move for its admission, but if we did that, that might be a better --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we'll use the witness's own markings and just reproduce them on our sets. The exhibit is marked now by the witness, and we'll just reproduce that. Thank you for your thought.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The marked map will be number P175.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I want to show you another map which is attached to P51/ID, 03266206. I just want you to identify that particular map for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Re. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What is that map?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're asking me the question? You can see that from the title. It's a categorisation of damage on facilities destroyed by war destruction in the Old Town of Dubrovnik of October and November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Is that a map which is in the Institute report P51/ID, but it's just a larger colour copy of it? A3 copy of what's in the Institute report.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this colour version. But I assume that it corresponds to the black and white one that I reviewed and that I used in my up-to-date inspections.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: A moment ago you said it was October-November. The title actually says "October, November, and December 1991." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did say "and December."

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The record is reflected. I just want this marked for identification for the moment. I understand there's a dispute as to the tendering of P51/ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can anticipate that dispute. But it merely leaves the Chamber with the question, which of these are December damage?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: That will ultimately be a matter of submission and, of course, weight of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, is this sourced to anything?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: P51/ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So that the problem is with P51? In fact, this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's a rather --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: My concern, Mr. Re, is that P51 is still not an exhibit for obvious reasons, and this would appear to be a summary of its total content.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, the reason for doing it this way is I'm asking the witness to identify -- identify this document being a larger from that exhibit. So if the exhibit goes in, it can go in as a large aide memoire for the Chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: At the moment, it will not rise any higher than P51. It will be marked for identification, Mr. Re. And you've still got a way to go to get it in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: We're working on it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: What I will ask you to do over the break is to take a copy of the large photograph which we tendered yesterday, and we have a list of buildings I will like you to mark on it, and a special purple pen. I want you to circle the buildings. I've listed them. And I've listed numbers next to them. If you could do that over the break and write in white on the right a legend, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 to 15, what the buildings are, noted in English - don't do it now - it would be very helpful. And I also wish to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic. Excuse me, Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like that any presentation of evidence is conducted before the Trial Chamber. If the witness is supposed to do anything according to a list from Mr. Re, I ask that the Chamber is part of that process to see what is being marked, how it's being marked. I can see that it's a list. I can see it from here. The Prosecutor is providing the witness with a list of what he's supposed to mark. Your Honours, let us see what this is about. Allow the witness to do this in front of us so that we are informed of each detail of that process of marking that is being expected of this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Petrovic. From the point of view of the Chamber, the witness is being invited in the break to mark on a map which is not yet an exhibit a list of a number of documents that are on a list that has been offered to him. If he does that, and his evidence is that he has done that, whether that document is admitted will depend then on his evidence about that list and what it signifies. And that is something we will explore after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: I'm just distributing a list -- a copy of the things I've asked him to mark.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And we will then ask the Court officer to do that which she has been anxious to do for some time; that is, to give the number for the map which is now marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The map marked for identification which is 03266206, that's the ERN number, is P176.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Your half hours continue to stretch, Mr. Re. I think we will have a break now and hopefully the matter can be concluded in a minute or two after the resumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Re.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: How did you go, Mr. Vukovic, in circling the large colour photograph of the buildings provided to you, the list of buildings in a number in the circle and writing a legend on the side in white? Would you just be able to put it on the overhead projector to your right so that we can all see how you went. The list which we circulated had 15 buildings to mark and 4 blocks to draw, to mark on the boundaries. How did you go?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, if I can just give additional clarification, or rather can I ask you for additional clarification. Could we have the date when this aerial image was made? I think that would be of interest in view of the comprehensiveness of information upon which this photograph Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. should be based. My second question is the following: I managed to mark all the buildings and blocks like you asked, but I have to ask you about building number 9, Institute office. Which particular locality do you have in mind? Because the institute office, this is actually the institute for the protection of cultural monuments, and it is in two different places. One of the localities is very close to the Dominican cloister. It's the one here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The one you're circling now.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then we can mark it now. That is number 9. And also a small technical correction. The city walls is not Pelinje, it is Peline, P-e-l-i-n-e. That would be it. Just another matter: I have added this on to this map as well. I don't know whether it will be visible enough. The situation is the same like on the photograph, but I think with a clear representation of the blocks and everything else that you wished to ask about, I think. As you could see, I did not manage to mark all the buildings in the legend. I came up to building number 4. So that would be it for the time being.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I propose this. If I complete my examination-in-chief now and the witness completes that during the cross-examination break, completing the marking of the -- the circling of the buildings and the marking of it, and it could be tendered later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I would like to know: What is this? What does this mean, this list that the Prosecutor gave to the witness asking him to circle all these buildings? What is the purpose of all of this? I have not seen anything from the exhibits that we've had so far that would show me what the purpose of this effort is. In order to be able -- for the witness to explain anything further or to have anything admitted into evidence, we need an explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I can only say that from the point of view of the Chamber, each of the blocks and buildings are ones that we recognise from the evidence of the witness. Is there a purpose beyond that, Mr. Re?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: No, it's simply identification of locality of buildings and locations the witness has referred to in his testimony and in the videos he identified. That's all. To give the Chamber a good overhead view of where these buildings are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That being so, Mr. Petrovic, it's merely another form of depiction of part of the evidence of the witness. And it's on that basis that it would be received. But we will have the witness complete the legend at a convenient time, and then we'll formally receive the map. That concludes your examination, does it?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And I thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Re. Mr. Petrovic. Perhaps it would be useful to remove the distractions from the witness at the moment and he can then concentrate on the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vukovic, I am Vladimir Petrovic, attorney-at-law, Defence counsel. I'm going to put a few questions to you in relation to your evidence before the Honourable Trial Chamber over these past few days. First of all, I would like to ask you something about this last list that you used for the markings. Let's start with this most recent development. There are 15 buildings on that list.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there are 15 buildings and 4 blocks.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please be so kind as to tell us whether it is your assertion that these 15 buildings were damaged on the 6th of December 1991. Is this the gist of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the gist of the question was. But what I answered, if that is considered to be testimony and evidence, then we could call it that. I can only confirm the buildings for which I know were certainly hit on the 6th. Since I was at these buildings or near them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Please focus on my questions. The buildings, the 15 ones on this list, some of them were hit on the 6th and some were not.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about some of them. Some of them were hit on the 6th and some were hit before the 6th. But I think that the ones hit before the 6th were a minority.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll deal with that later. Please tell us briefly, what was the exact job title you held in the institution that you were employed in in September 1991 and onwards?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. What was the date? I didn't manage to catch that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: September 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the responsible town planner in the town planning institute, the Institute for Planning and Environment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, this institute, this service, is it -- or rather was it an integral part of the then municipal assembly of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was the only institution at the level of the former municipality of Dubrovnik and it was engaged in the elaboration of town plans.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, where was your particular service?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Our building, and therefore the service, too, if you meant the physical locality --

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- it was in Lapad, near Gospino Polje, that is to say in the immediate vicinity of Put Ive Vojnovica. If you're familiar with Dubrovnik, it is from the Hotel Lero towards Lapad.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Tell me, where was the municipal assembly of Dubrovnik? Where was its building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The municipal assembly building was in the Old Town. This is a locality which is above the City Cafe so that you would know where it is, or rather the town theatre is, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Between the bell tower and the rector's palace. Right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You told us that at the moment when you first found out about these events in Dubrovnik that you were at a meeting of the executive council of the municipal assembly of Dubrovnik. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The executive council. Those would be the right words, yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In what capacity did you attend the meeting?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my capacity as the responsible town planner. I was elaborating on a town plan which was then supposed to enter the procedure of being adopted by the municipal assembly. Specifically, it had to do with the peninsula of Babin Kuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where were these meetings held? Or rather, where was this meeting held?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This meeting was held on the premises of the building you referred to, that is to say on the first floor, I think, and that was the premises where the executive council of the then municipality of Dubrovnik used to meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So that is the building between the bell tower and the rector's palace?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of the executive council?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Zeljko Sikic president of the executive council?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at that time Zeljko Sikic president of the executive council.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Sikic president of the council throughout this period of the time that we're talking about here, that is to say, October, November, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did I understand this correctly, did I understand your statement correctly when you said that you last attended a meeting of the executive Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. council on the day when the hostilities started in the territory of the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular wording could be put as follows: That at that moment, the meeting of the executive council was interrupted, adjourned. It was a Tuesday. I remember that Tuesday well. And it was around 12.00. That is something I remember. Now, whether it was official hostility vis-a-vis Dubrovnik is something that I cannot interpret but at that point in time that is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, at that time in 1991, or rather after that point in time, it is quite understandable that you did not attend meetings of the executive council any longer?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not because all activities were ceased. All activities that had to do with the official activities that we as the institute were supposed to perform for the municipality until that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the further activities of the executive council in that period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know. For your information, you should be using the word executive council, not executive board.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. You are -- perhaps the problem is that we are using similar languages, and this is the word that we use in our language.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A board is a bit lower than council. We did have boards, too, but they were at a lower level.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So we're talking about the executive council which is a city government, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. A city government, a town government, the executive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, we need to pause between question and answer for the interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for having cautioned me, Your Honour. I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, do you know Mr. Sikic personally?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew him personally to the extent that we were in contact in relation to various official communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in this period of October, November, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember well that at that time I was working on a town plan for the big marina in Dubrovnik, in the Harbour of Gruz. In that period, this was sometime around the month of June, if I remember correctly, that is when this was supposed to be adopted by the municipal assembly, and I can say with certainty now that this was the moment when we got to know each other a bit better. So we would see each other from time to time, but it had to do with that particular matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please focus on my questions as much as possible. I'm asking you about these three months, October, November, December 1991.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you with any certainty because my memory doesn't serve me very well any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what a crisis staff is? What the crisis staff of the Municipality of Dubrovnik is?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I could infer at that moment as an inhabitant of Dubrovnik, it was a body that was supposed to coordinate life in the city in a way in the extraordinary situation that came to be when the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who the members of the crisis staff were?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would it perhaps be of assistance if I told you that Mr. Sikic was one of the prominent members of that crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. I'm not sure if that's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us in this period of time, October, November, December, that is, for how many days were there attacks or any kind of operations on, in, and around the town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must tell you that I did not keep a diary, so I cannot answer you with any degree of precision. But I can just give you my general impression. I know that from the summer and moving towards the 6th, the intensity of hostilities went up in terms of shelling and generally speaking the atmosphere in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You referred to shelling, or rather bombardment. How do you understand this what you call bombardment or shelling in the period from October to December 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only confirm on the basis of my memory -- I mean, I was in Lapad for the most time then. And I was not at all these different localities, so I'm only going to talk about the things I witnessed myself. As far as the shelling was concerned, so I will confine myself first to the locality where I was an actual eyewitness and secondly I heard things over the radio and people who were in direct contact. So I cannot give you the exact figure. I can just tell you that there was this progression. And as it progressed from the summer towards the 6th of December, the intensity was increased. The locality that was shelled in my neighbourhood was the reporting centre. I think I referred to that in my initial statement, and I think that this is something that I experienced rather intensively. Also, I saw the shelling of Srdj and also I saw these aircraft projectiles from the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say from the summer, what month are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I think it was already in August that something was happening when one airplane of the Yugoslav Army flew at a low altitude by the town of Dubrovnik. We thought that this did not auger well for the future. It was probably a reconnaissance flight or something like that. After that, there were only individual cases, sporadic ones, and then there were more and more as we move towards the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When did these cases of individual, sporadic bombardment or shelling take place, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was sometime in the month of October, November. November was already shocking for us because even the Old Town was targeted then. So that would be an answer to your question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: If I were to tell you that during those three months, there was a total of four days of what you call bombardment or shelling, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a few minutes ago that I cannot speak with any degree of precision about the number of days or shells or hours. I didn't keep a diary. And my memory does not serve me that well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But is it possible there was only four days?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an answer with any degree of certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What's the address of your mother's place in Old Town in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She lives in Poljana Buniceva. That's near the cathedral.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What's your mother's address?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's Buniceva Poljana, and I think it's either 6 or 4. I don't know exactly at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wondered -- I'm a little surprised that you don't know your mother's address.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these addresses changed since when I was there. It was 4 in the beginning, and then later it was 6. It was just the land surveyors' office designation, so it was either 4 or 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what the number of the house is today where your mother lives in Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is Buniceva Poljana number 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was your mother's house damaged?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Luckily, it was not damaged much, but it did have indirect hit damage from a projectile which fell in the vicinity and destroyed the front doors as well as the glass on the first floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And can you tell us how did this house number change in Old Town? Why did it change and when? How come that it changed from 4 to 6? Was something new built there? Was there a new building? Were buildings issued with new numbers or something like that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think the number change probably came about for statistical or land surveying office reasons. When they were placing stone number markings, then at the time the sequence that was recorded in the cadastre office was also stuck to there. So I think that this change really is of minor significance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Isn't it strange that such a trivial question such as the address on which you lived and at which your mother lives is something that you are not sure about?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we're talking about the number. Why is that so significant? If you're asking me about exactly which building she is in, I'm the visual type. I can tell you exactly which building that is. So that is Buniceva Poljana 6 or number 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you because you showed us here at least 63 buildings claiming that these are the exact building numbers as it states in Exhibit Number --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not get the number of the exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you're saying about these buildings you know something for certain. But as far as the place where you lived or where your mother lived, you say that you are not sure?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the moment when we were conducting the inspections, we were focussed on certain information that we required at the moment, including the house number which we were supposed to identify and inspect. So this is what we were focussed on at the time. So it is quite understandable that this is a piece of information which is reliable and which represents something that is true. And specifically, my mother's house is a building that suffered an indirect hit with shrapnel, so it was never handled as a damaged building. We just thought that it was something that did not have the same significance as some of the other damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you well, you did not register your mother's building?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not part of our inspection. The buildings, it did not have the same extent of damage as the other buildings did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: We will come to that later, and we will see whether this is so or not. You said that after learning that bombardment as you called it started, you said that you went to your office, and that you took steps to protect books. What exactly did you do? What were the books that you were protecting? You were protecting them from what? And how did you protect them?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, it was our duty to protect the material that we had in the department of urban planning from potential damage which was sort of announced due to the bombing. I'm talking about new maps, which is the basis for urban planning, many urban plans, so it was our duty in a way to protect and preserve these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Where did you do that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did that in the building of our institute, and it was near Gospino Polje which I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you did this every day.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We came every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me put the question to you first. This was a job that you did every day until the time that we are talking about, until December and the events which we were discussing earlier.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: How often did you go to the Old Town and to see your mother in that period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the 6th of December, I went on average once a week. But we were in touch more often by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Was the telephone working throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, luckily it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us very briefly, what route did you take from your apartment, from Ive Vojnovica 104 to the Old Town, to your mother's place?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two routes. If you know the route, one of them was Ive Vojnovica Street. That is quite a large street linking the area of Lapad and the part towards Old Town. And that's the route I most frequently took. Mostly walking on the side which was less exposed to the site at Zarkovica. Then I went along Cingria [phoen], Ulica, and passed by the old hospital, came down to Pile, and then would enter the Old Town and took a shortcut to the institute. So that was the route. And along with that, we also used another route which goes on the other side of the Montovjerna hill. That street today is called Ban Jelacic Street. I don't know what it was called at the time. I don't remember any more. So that was also another parallel direction to Cingria.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So these were the two directions that you used when going to Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were the two main routes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And this third one was an alternative route?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this one was Ive Vojnovica through Cingria, to Boninovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ante Statevica?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's -- it's called Ante Statevica now. That's the street. I considered that to be one route.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you move around the town of Dubrovnik other than these regular visits to your mother?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In this period, does that mean that you did not go anywhere from your flat in Lapad except to go to work, which is nearby, and to visit your mother in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was mostly the area within which I moved, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: You lived in Ive Vojnovica number 104?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. And I'm still living there now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us where the information centre was or the alerting centre that you talked about.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was across the street, to the south of the building where I lived, in the immediate vicinity of the new hospital. That's the area of Gorica Sveto Vlaho, so it's above the sea.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When you say information centre, what is that, what kind of a facility was that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was a facility also before the war for the assembling of certain information and providing certain information. But I don't know exactly what this was all about. It was a kind of working name that I heard, and that's how I interpreted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What kind of information are we talking about? Is this intelligence information or what kind of information? What do you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't really know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that your street, Ive Vojnovica Street in this period that we're talking about was exposed to quite strong, intense shelling?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite intense shelling. On the 6th of December specifically, and it was so intense that we even named it is the Vukovar neighbourhood because the level of the intensity was such and the effects were such that it was really terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber what do you mean by the Vukovar neighbourhood? Is that a synonym for major destruction?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, and it relates to the town of Vukovar which up until then was a kind of example of such terrible destruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us who was shelling your street and where did the shells come from.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shells evidently came from the eastern side. I don't know exactly where from. But according to some information I heard that there was firing from Zarkovica, from Zvekovica, that there were tank grenades as well that were being used, the impacts were quite strong. I even remember one man who was killed. I didn't see him, but I did see the car that he was in at the time when the shell struck it. It was all burned out. My apartment was partially destroyed by shrapnel. Excuse me. That was one source in that period. And I'm not sure whether there was anything behind the hill of Srdj from Strincjera. So that was from the northern side, if I can sort of describe the direction more closely. I don't know whether there was anything coming from the direction of the sea. I know that in that block of ours, we were concerned from danger from the seaside. I'm not sure, though, whether anything really did come from that direction or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And did you hear whether any part of town was actually shelled from the sea?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not specifically hear whether it was from the sea, but I know that there was a danger coming from there. I don't know whether this was really so or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned Zvekovica. That is above Cavtat, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is an area -- when I say Zvekovica, you can take that to mean that it's a broader sector, and it indicates the environs where we could maybe term that it came from. So when we say Zvekovica, that's the area I mean, but I'm not able to tell you what weapons we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that the shelling was progressive, that it would start at one end of the street and then go on from one house to the next. That's how you described it. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at one point, I don't know exactly what time of the day this was, I know that things would start out with lesser intensity, and then at some point of the day, they would start substantial shelling in a way that the place of impact in the line of fire would move by 10, 15, or 20 metres forward. So that would be the sequence of strikes that we could recall at that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the shells would move forward by 10 or 20 metre increments?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not sure about the distance. But this is just a layman's estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: But that's the gist of it, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: And you said that all the cars in the streets were destroyed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. They were destroyed. I apologise. Yes. All the cars were burned in that section. And there were also some casualties that I mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Could you please tell us, before the conflict broke out in the area of Dubrovnik, was any JNA unit located there according to what you know?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my recollection, I didn't hear of anything like that. When you're talking about the town area, what do you mean? Do you mean the broader area of the town or the inner centre?

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When I say the town of Dubrovnik, I mean the town from the Hotel Belvedere to the Komolac Stjepan, including Lapad, Gruz, Babin Kuk, Old Town. This is the part of town that I mean.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That area is something different. I already said that Zarkovica was the point -- if I have understood the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: No, you did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, then I apologise. Could you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Before the conflict broke out, before September, before August -- before August 1991, in that area, from Hotel Belvedere to the Gruz harbour, were there any JNA units located there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, no. But of course I say "as far as I know."

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Of course. We're only talking about the things that you know. Could you please tell us, in the period October, November, and December in this demarcated area of the town of Dubrovnik, where were the Croatian Army weapons situated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of any position of the Croatian Army in this area as we have delineated it now? Just now, in the period of October, November, and December?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was more like a story, but I didn't really have any reliable information. It was mostly something that was supposed to respond to this attack. So I think it was somewhere at Glavica or thereabouts. That is all that I knew at the time. It was a layman's information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: The layman's information that you had at Ilinija Glavica, that the area of Bogosica Park?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure whether it's the area of Bogosica Park exactly, but it's in that sector. I think that Ilinija Glavica includes that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Ilinija Glavica is within the near vicinity of Bogosica Park?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What did you hear about Ilinija Glavica?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Could we just clarify for the record whether Glavica and Ilinija Glavica the same place? I note in the transcript Mr. Petrovic -- sorry, the answer at 47.15 was it was at Glavica, thereabouts, and then the question was, the layman's information you had, Ilinija Glavica. I just want to clarify we're talking about the same place.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vukovic, we have all the while been talking about Ilinija Glavica, haven't we?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it written down here in a wrong manner. It was the church of St. Ilija, and it was after that church that the hill was named Ilinija Glavica. Therefore, this is the correct definition of the locality I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: So the two of us have all the while been talking about Ilinija Glavica as part of Bogosica Park?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I can't really say that Bogosica Park would come exclusively under Ilinija Glavica, but it does come under a part of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Tell us, do you know which positions of the Croatian Army were there?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: In the period of October, November, and December in 1991 in Dubrovnik, did you ever see any armed people around?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my movements were quite limited. I've already stated this. And within the area that I moved in, I do not recall ever seeing armed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you see anyone wearing a uniform of the Croatian Army or the Croatian police in that period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to recollect.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of anyone who was drafted into the Croatian Army in that period?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know of some of my friends, several of my friends who were apparently wearing a uniform, but this is something I learned eventually.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you please be so kind as to tell us what you found out eventually.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we found out that these people were on positions defending Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were you told where these positions were?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't discuss that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were these people, these friends of yours armed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did the Croatian Army in Dubrovnik have its own artillery?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear the activity of Croatian Army from Dubrovnik on the JNA positions?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was very difficult to conclude that from what we would hear and to actually identify whether the source of the fire that was opened came from the JNA or the other side. I can only say with some certainty that I was unable to distinguish at the time what constituted an impact and what constituted fire being opened from the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any positions of the Croatian Army in your street, in Ive Vojnovica Street?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Were there any Croatian Army artillery positions in your street, Ive Vojnovica Street?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer again is I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Would you be surprised if I told you that in your street, in Ive Vojnovica Street, the main artillery position of the Croatian Army was stationed in the period of October, November, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I hear of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the command post of the Croatian Army artillery was situated in your street in the period of October, November, December 1991?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hear this information for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: When passing down your street, Ive Vojnovica Street, did you ever see the artillery pieces of the Croatian Army?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: Did anyone ever open fire from the Croatian side, from your street, Ive Vojnovica Street?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN VUKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago that I was unable to identify the source of explosions in order for me to be able to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: What would you tell me if I told you that in your street the most important position of the artillery of the Croatian Army was situated in -- on the 6th of December 1991?
